idiom_name: paper_trail version_at / reify over a versions table
implementation_notes: In Rails the realization is has_paper_trail: every save writes a PaperTrail::Version row holding the object as it was before the change, and widget.paper_trail.version_at(1.day.ago) returns the model as it looked at that timestamp (it reifies the first version created after it; version.reify builds the object, versions_between(t1, t2) collects the states over an interval, and where_object queries a versioned attribute's historical value). What replaces the classic structure: the versions table plus version_at/reify - the model keeps ordinary attribute readers. Outside ActiveRecord, or when the index is a business effective date, a hash keyed by Date plus a sorted keys array answers the same question in a few lines, because Date/Time are Comparable (ActiveSupport even makes Date and Time comparable across types).
code_sketch:
class Employee < ApplicationRecord
  has_paper_trail only: %i[salary]
end

employee = Employee.find(id)
employee.paper_trail.version_at(Date.new(2024, 4, 1))   # the object as it was then
employee.versions.where_object(salary: 12_000).count    # versions holding that value
employee.paper_trail.versions_between(2.years.ago, Date.today).map(&:created_at)
pitfalls: A version stores the object as it was before the change, so version_at(t) looks for the first version created after t; two updates in the same second share created_at and the boundary pick becomes order-dependent.

paper_trail records transaction time (created_at of the version), not business validity: a correction back-dated to April is stored now, so an explicit effective-date column is required for as-of business questions.
reify returns a live model instance - saving it reverts the record - and columns added after a version was written reify as nil unless unversioned_attributes is configured.

Versions accumulate one row per save: without PaperTrail's cleanup (or partition pruning) the table dominates the database, and version models are read through the same connection, so point-in-time queries compete with application traffic.
